title: Cast your care (1 Peter 5:7)
hookLine: casting all your care upon him, for he hath care of you

cards: On the road into Jerusalem, a few days before he dies, Jesus needs something to ride. The disciples bring a young colt, and Luke says they throw their cloaks onto it and set Jesus on top. Throw.

Not fold, not drape. They toss their coats on the animal's back, the way you'd sling a bag onto a bed after a long day. Peter uses the same Greek verb near the end of his first letter, and he isn't talking about coats.

teach.b: Here's the verse in the Douay-Rheims: "Casting all your care upon him, for he hath care of you." Casting: throwing it on, the way the disciples threw their cloaks onto the colt.
Not a polite handing over, but a toss, the move of someone who's been carrying something too long.
And it's all your care, not just the small worries you'd be willing to share. Notice the word care appears twice, and in Greek it's two different words.
The first is merimna: anxiety, worry that won't sit still. Jesus uses the same family of words in the Sermon on the Mount, when he tells his followers not to be anxious about tomorrow.
The second is softer: it matters to him. Literally, you are a concern to him. So the sentence runs: throw your anxiety on him, because you matter to him.
The reason isn't that worry is foolish. The reason is that someone cares. Peter didn't invent this.
He's echoing the psalms, which the Douay-Rheims renders: "Cast thy care upon the Lord, and he shall sustain thee." And look at the verse just before: be humbled under the mighty hand of God.
In Peter's order, casting your care is a kind of humility: admitting you can't carry everything alone, and letting someone else take the weight.

teach.h: FOR HE HATH CARE OF YOU.
teach.b: Catholic spiritual writers have a name for the habit: abandonment to God's providence.

how: Catholics bring their worries to God in personal prayer, in intentions offered at Mass and in devotions of trust in Divine Providence; the tradition calls the habit of entrusting everything to God abandonment to providence.

o: a careful plan for what comes next
the cloak thrown onto the colt
anxiety, worry that won't sit still

games.q: cast your care — tap the pairs.
p: throw it on, like cloaks on a colt

s: Peter says to hand God the small worries and keep the big ones
the word care appears twice in the verse, and in Greek they're two different words
first anxiety, merimna; then 'it matters to him'.
the verb cast here means to set something down gently
it means to throw it on, the same verb as the cloaks thrown onto the colt in Luke.

games.q: a worry has been riding on your shoulders for weeks. you've told no one. what does Peter tell you to do with it?
o: carry it until it's solved, so you don't burden anyone.
throw all of it on God, because he cares for you.
share only the parts that seem small enough.
games.why: casting all your care upon him: all of it, thrown, not placed. and right before, Peter calls that humility.

practice: Name the one worry that has ridden with you most this week, and picture it as something you can hold: a heavy bag, a stone, a knot of rope.
Then, on an out-breath, imagine tossing it, not placing it carefully, onto someone stronger.
If you pray, say Peter's line, casting all your care upon him, and leave it there; if not, just notice what your shoulders do when you put it down.

wordCard.voice: Merimna, anxiety. First Peter five: throw your worry on God, the way the disciples threw their cloaks on the colt, because you matter to him. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: anxiety, worry (1 Peter 5:7). Jesus uses the same family of words in Matthew 6: be not anxious.

carryVoice: Your line: he hath care of you. All of it, tossed like a cloak. Day six hundred ten.
